content: Between 2010 and 2014, nearly 600 million adults aged 15 and older accessed HIV testing services in 122 lowand middle-income countries. In 2014 alone, approximately 150 million individuals, including children, men, and women, received HIV testing and their results in 129 such countries. This significant scale-up was facilitated in part by the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), which have been instrumental in expanding HIV testing services (HTS), particularly in resource-limited settings where laboratory access is restricted. RDTs prequalified by the World Health Organization (WHO) demonstrate a diagnostic and clinical sensitivity of at least 99% and a specificity of 98%. The performance of these RDTs, when used within a WHO-recommended testing strategy and a validated national testing algorithm, has been shown to be highly reliable. However, many countries have not implemented quality management systems that align with the scale-up of HTS. They have also failed to utilize WHO-prequalified RDTs or adopt WHO-recommended testing strategies. A recent analysis of HIV testing policies in 48 countries revealed that only 20% of testing strategies adhered to current WHO recommendations. There is an increasing number of reports highlighting poor-quality HIV testing, which has led to misdiagnoses of HIV status. Misdiagnoses can occur in two forms: falsely identifying an HIV-positive individual as HIV-negative or vice versa. Audits in some settings have revealed substantial levels of false-positive diagnoses. Misdiagnoses can result from limitations in the assay itself, operator-related errors, facility-related issues such as improper storage of reagents, selection of inappropriate testing strategies, and suboptimal national testing algorithms. Additionally, workload factors, such as high client volumes leading to overburdened staff or low client volumes resulting in poor proficiency, can contribute to errors. Inadequate training and lack of supportive supervision further exacerbate operator errors. In many countries, errors in HIV testing may go undetected and uncorrected due to the absence of comprehensive quality management systems or adequate external quality assessment. The consequences of such misdiagnoses are severe. A false-negative HIV status represents a failure to correctly diagnose a client, link them to prevention, treatment, and care services, and prevent ongoing HIV transmission. Conversely, a false-positive HIV diagnosis can lead to unnecessary initiation of lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART), potential stigma, discrimination, and criminalization. It also limits the availability of interventions to prevent HIV infection, harms community and family relationships, and, if the results are later found to be incorrect, undermines the credibility of test results and trust in health services. Incorrectly initiating ART wastes scarce resources, including medicine stocks, clinic and staff time, and laboratory tests for ART monitoring, such as viral load assessments. This issue is particularly concerning in settings where clients are offered immediate ART initiation after receiving an HIV-positive result, regardless of CD4 count or clinical assessment. If left unaddressed, these quality issues and misdiagnoses could undermine the global HIV response and hinder progress toward achieving new global targets, such as correctly diagnosing 90% of people with HIV by 2020, preventing new HIV infections, and providing treatment to those living with HIV. To address these challenges, a systematic literature review was conducted to assess the causes and extent of HIV misdiagnoses in various settings. The review included studies from multiple countries and regions, examining factors such as test kit performance, operator errors, testing strategies, population characteristics, and testing site conditions. The findings highlighted the need for improved quality management systems, adherence to WHO-recommended testing strategies, and robust external quality assessments to ensure accurate HIV diagnosis and effective linkage to care.
